TO THE CITIZENS OF VIRGINIA.

Once more to the breach, my friends!" To the polls—and we will be victorious. Our news from all parts of the State is cheering. Counties in which we did not even dare to hope that our friends would show themselves, are putting forth their strength—and they expect to be victorious. YESTERDAY we heard of several of this description; and everywhere our friends are in the finest spirits seeing what old Sussex has done. Our political associates promise us equal success in other counties. They are making head against the friends of the Bank or the weak, wavering professors of the Constitution in their very strongholds. Let the real, unhesitating, incorruptible, unequivocating friends of the Constitution, do their duty, and all will be well. The Northern Neck—the South side—the Mid country—the region beyond the Ridge—are expected to rally around the principles of '98—the Bank principles of Jefferson and his associates. Let every man do his duty—and the scourge of the People: the far-born monster of federalism!" that tremendous institution which like the deadly nightshade threatens to blight our liberties and our State Rights as it has already violated and ensued the Constitution will be put down by the indignant voice of a free People. No National Bank at all, ought to be our motto—Prolong the monster, and you perpetuate it. Not they should be given TO extend its charter: But seize it with strong arm, and strangle its charter. Upon your voice, Freemen of Virginia, all now depends. In your Legislature gloriously asserted the "sovereignty of your State," and instructed our Senators to protest against renewal of the old Bank; when the monster perished—Send his men equally determined to assert your rights, next winter, and the same people will warn you that that plan is on foot to extricate the charter of this Bank. If you do not return good and true men, that deed will be accomplished and the darkest day which this Republic ever saw, will come upon us.

The House of Representatives have done their duty—On Friday last there was long and violent struggle in the House of Representatives, but the final vote on the resolutions of the Committee of Ways and Means TAKEN. The first resolution, declaring that the bank ought not to be re-chartered was carried by vote of 187 to 50. The second, that the deposites ought not to be restored by the Treasury. The third resolution, that the State Banks ought to be continued as the "places of deposite of the public money, and that it is expedient for Congress TO make further provisions by law, prescribing the mode of selection, the securities to be taken, and the manner and terms on which they are to be employed," carried by vote of 112 to 105. And the 4th resolution, for committee to examine into the causes of the present distress, and the abuses of the Bank prevailed by vote of 14 to 11. Now then will the curtain be drawn up and the abuses of this corrupt Institution will be unveiled to the public eye. A strong COMMITTEE will be appointed to scrutinize its acts—and unveil its Vaccinations against the Press, against members of Congress—its bad Councillors in the branches as well as the mother Bank. The light of day will be let in upon all its dark transactions—its friends tremble for it—and we shall once more have cause to thank Andrew Jackson for the courage he has displayed.

We congratulate you on the votes of the House, for we have gloriously triumphed. We have silenced those men, who were crying up the other day, the votes of the sixty-six Senators—some of whom are going in direct opposition to the wishes and instructions of their constituents. But here we have the votes of the immediate representatives of the people, to whom is peculiarly entrusted the revenue of the people, and who alone can originate, under the Constitution, revenue BILLS.

This great battle then is over at last—63 against re-chartering the Bank. The deposites not to be restored. The State Banks to be made the Depositories of the public money, under certain regulations of Congress—and committee TO be appointed TO bring to light the outrageous conduct of the Bank and expose its enormities to the world. So much for months discussion! and all the battle and boasting in Congress, of Presidential aspirants and disappointing demagogues, since the commencement of this most extraordinary session of Congress—

The immediate Representatives of the People have obeyed their will and rolled back the wave of popular Indignation upon the unprincipled lenders in the Senate and their servile followers, who have notoriously put at defiance the Instructions of their constituents. We differed with the Executive as to the policy of removing the public deposites at the Treasury, and in the manner the removal was made. But the Bank has gone on in style against the Government, and has really manifested a spirit of dictation to the constituted authorities, which ought to make the blood run warm in the veins of every free citizen in the United States. Do we want the Government of the People or the Government of the Bank! is really the simple question.

The friends of the President in Congress are all in the highest spirits, and exulting at the triumphant victory they have obtained in favor of free Government. It is for free People now to second their virtuous efforts.

Upon the People, now, everything depends. Your representatives have done their duty; and will not you support them? Will you not help them to put down this unconstitutional Bank—and preserve your State Banks from its power? Citizens of Virginia, this question comes home to your business and your Domains.—To the Polls, then, TO the Polls!
